meaning: To abandon or desert someone; to jilt a lover, or to reject a friend, ally or plan in favour of another.
note: Commonest use is romantic — 'she threw him over for a richer man'. Also 'throw over a scheme' = give it up.

meaning: To give up, admit defeat and abandon an undertaking (from throwing in one's hand at cards).
note: Non-standard heading: the idiom is 'throw up ONE'S cards' (or 'throw in one's cards' / 'throw in one's hand'). Meaning is secure; the wording is a deck truncation.

meaning: Literally to fish with rod and line; figuratively, to try to obtain something indirectly, by hints, flattery or scheming rather than by asking outright — 'to angle for a compliment / an invitation'.
note: In idiom decks the intended sense is nearly always the figurative one: to fish for something by artifice.

meaning: Two established senses: (1) to be at ease, comfortable and unembarrassed in a place or company; (2) to be thoroughly conversant with a subject — 'he is at home in higher mathematics'. A third, older sense is to be in and ready to receive visitors.
note: Exam decks usually target sense (2), 'well-versed in'.

meaning: To defy openly; to challenge or set at naught, refusing to submit — 'to bid defiance to authority'.
note: Often extended to inanimate resistance: a fort that bids defiance to attack, i.e. successfully withstands it.

meaning: To have effects in two opposite directions — an argument or circumstance that tells for one side as much as against it, or a benefit that carries an equal drawback.
note: CORRUPTION: the real idiom is 'to cut both ways'. The heading has probably crossed it with 'burn the candle at both ends' (= exhaust oneself by overwork or dissipation). Meaning given is for 'cut both ways'.

meaning: To stop idle chatter and get down to business; to come to the point.
note: From the fuller 'cut the cackle and come to the horses'.

meaning: To seek only the pleasures of life while avoiding its pains and duties — to take the flowers and leave the thorns.
note: Not a standard English idiom I can vouch for; the reading above is the transparent figurative one and matches the rose/thorn convention. Treat as low-weight evidence.

idiom: To get more kicks than half pence
meaning: To receive far more abuse and ill-treatment than reward; to come off badly, with blows instead of pay.
note: Standard form is 'more kicks than halfpence', from performing animals or beggars who were kicked more often than they were given coins.

meaning: To look dejected, downcast or dismayed; of a situation or prospect, to appear discouraging and unpromising.
note: Both the personal sense ('he looked blue at the news') and the impersonal ('things look blue') are current.

meaning: To fight a duel; hence to engage in a contest with an opponent, testing one's strength or ability against his.
note: From the literal pre-duel practice of comparing blades for equal length.

idiom: To put one out of countenance
meaning: To disconcert or abash someone; to embarrass a person so that he loses his composure and self-possession.
note: 'Countenance' here is calm self-assurance of face, not merely the face.

idiom: To put one’s hand to plough
meaning: To set about a task in earnest; to commit oneself wholeheartedly to an undertaking (with the implication that one should not then look back).
note: Slight non-standard wording — usually 'put one's hand to THE plough'. Biblical, Luke 9:62: 'No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.'

meaning: To disparage someone; to speak ill of a person, belittling him behind his back.
note: Two rival literal senses exist — to knock down with a vehicle, and to pursue and overtake — but in an idiom list the defamation sense is the intended one.

meaning: To give warning of grave and imminent danger; to raise the alarm about a serious approaching threat.
note: Non-standard heading. English normally has 'sound the alarm' or 'be on red alert'; 'sound red alert' looks like a deck's own coinage. The meaning above is nonetheless unambiguous.

meaning: To cover every aspect of a matter and consult everyone concerned, leaving no detail or person overlooked.
note: American, from baseball, where a runner must touch each base in turn for a run to count. Often 'touch base with someone' = make contact.

meaning: To reject or refuse — an offer, request, application or suitor. Secondarily, to reduce the level of something (volume, heat, light).
note: Exam decks want 'reject'.

meaning: To arrive or appear, often unexpectedly or after a delay; also, of a lost thing, to be found. Secondarily, to increase (volume, heat).
note: Also 'something will turn up' = a chance or opportunity will present itself.

meaning: Made him conceited and vain; success or flattery went to his head and destroyed his good sense and modesty.
note: Heading is lifted mid-sentence; lemma is 'to turn someone's head'. A weaker second sense — to infatuate, to make someone fall in love — also exists, but the vanity sense is primary.

meaning: Anywhere in the world; in existence at all. Used as an intensifier after 'everything', 'nothing', 'who/what' — 'he has tried every remedy under the sun'.
note: From Ecclesiastes, 'there is no new thing under the sun'.

meaning: Held secretly in reserve — a plan, resource or advantage kept hidden and ready to be produced when needed ('he still has a trick up his sleeve').
note: Non-standard plural: the idiom is singular, 'up one's SLEEVE'. If the plural is deliberate the heading may instead be a truncation of 'roll up one's sleeves' = to prepare oneself for hard work, which is a completely different meaning. Flagging as ambiguous.

meaning: In relation to, with regard to, as compared with; also, face to face with, or a person/thing occupying a corresponding position (a counterpart).
note: Not an idiom but a French borrowing, properly 'vis-à-vis' (literally 'face to face'). The 'in relation to' sense is the ordinary modern one.

meaning: To mourn a lost love; to grieve for a sweetheart who has died or has deserted or jilted one.
note: Usually just 'wear the willow'. The willow is the traditional emblem of forsaken love — Desdemona's willow song in Othello, and the older ballad 'All a green willow is my garland'.

meaning: Contributed greatly towards a result; helped substantially to bring something about. Of money or supplies, lasted well and did much service.
note: Heading is a mid-sentence lift; lemma is 'to go a long way (towards something)'. Distinguish from 'go a long way' said of a person = to be very successful in life.

meaning: Was abandoned or utterly disregarded; was scattered and lost, coming to nothing.
note: Non-standard heading. The real forms are 'throw/cast/fling to the winds' (= abandon recklessly, as in 'threw caution to the winds') and 'gone with the wind' (= vanished for good). 'Went to the winds' reads like a deck's blend of the two, so the direction of the meaning — deliberate abandonment vs mere disappearance — is not recoverable from the heading alone.

meaning: To put on a show of courage or confidence while actually afraid or uncertain; to try to keep up one's spirits in a frightening or hopeless situation.
note: From the literal habit of whistling to steady one's nerves in a dark place.

meaning: Rough, crude and uncivilised; lawless and unpolished, in the manner of the old American frontier.
note: From 'the wild and woolly West'; 'woolly' alluding to unfinished sheepskin worn hair-side out.

meaning: UNKNOWN
note: I cannot settle this one honestly. Candidates: (a) old cant 'to wipe a person's nose' = to cheat or dupe him; (b) a corruption of 'to wipe someone's EYE' = to outdo or forestall a rival, get the better of him; (c) a literal mid-sentence lift with no idiomatic force at all. I cannot distinguish between them, so recording UNKNOWN rather than a plausible guess. Heading is also a mid-sentence lift — no 'one's'.

meaning: To turn out well in the end, to succeed or be resolved satisfactorily; also to solve or calculate, to devise (a plan), and to take physical exercise.
note: Idiom decks usually want 'turn out successfully' — 'everything worked out in the end'.
